title: Sea Dragons Older Than Dinosaurs
place: Flowerdalen, Isfjorden, Spitsbergen, Svalbard, Norway
text: In 2014, fossil hunters on Spitsbergen collected rock nodules in Flower's Valley on the southern shore of Ice Fjord. Inside were 11 linked tail bones from an ichthyosaur, a dolphin-shaped 'fish-lizard'. Dated to about two million years after Earth's worst mass extinction, they are the oldest ichthyosaur fossils known. They match much bigger, later species, hinting that these sea reptiles began before the extinction.

source.name: Uppsala University: Oldest sea reptile from Age of Dinosaurs found on Arctic island

title: A Frog Pond in Antarctica's Forests
place: La Meseta Formation, Seymour Island, Antarctic Peninsula, Antarctica
text: Around 40 million years ago, Antarctica still had ponds among southern beech forests. On Seymour Island, Argentinian and Swedish teams working from 2011 to 2013 found a hip bone and a skull fragment from a helmeted frog, the first modern amphibian ever found in Antarctica. Its closest living relatives live in Chile's damp forests today, so even the coldest month there likely stayed above about 3.75°C.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): First fossil frog from Antarctica

title: Ice That Fell Six Million Years Ago
place: Allan Hills blue ice area, Victoria Land, East Antarctica
text: The deepest continuous Antarctic ice core reaches back 800,000 years. But in the Allan Hills, a bare 'blue ice' area brings jumbled ancient ice near the surface. Shallow cores drilled to bedrock there, up to 206 metres down, held ice and trapped air that scientists dated by their argon content: up to 6 million years old. Its chemistry shows Antarctica has cooled about 12°C since then.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Miocene and Pliocene ice and air from the Allan Hills blue ice area, East Antarctica

title: When North Greenland Was 8°C Warmer
place: NEEM ice core camp, North Greenland Ice Sheet, Greenland
text: Drilling more than 2.4 kilometres to bedrock, scientists from 14 nations at the NEEM camp recovered the first complete ice record of the Eemian, a warm spell about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago. North Greenland was then about 8°C warmer than today, and summer meltwater refroze into layers in the snow. Yet the ice surface sat only a few hundred metres lower, so Antarctica must have raised seas too.

source.name: University of Washington News: Greenland ice core provides picture of prehistoric sea level rise

title: Grandfather of the Huskies
place: Zhokhov Island, New Siberian Islands, Russia
text: About 9,500 years ago, a dog lived on tiny Zhokhov Island in the Siberian Arctic. In 2020, scientists read its full genome, the oldest complete dog genome yet sequenced. Siberian Huskies, Alaskan Malamutes and Greenland sledge dogs share most of their DNA with it, pushing sledge-dog origins back thousands of years. Like polar bears and Arctic peoples, these dogs carry adaptations for a high-fat diet.

source.name: Trinity College Dublin: Scientists sequence oldest complete dog genome, 9,500-year-old Siberian sledge dog Zhokov

title: Sixty Million Nests on the Seabed
place: Southern Weddell Sea, off the Filchner Ice Shelf, Antarctica
text: In early 2021, the icebreaker Polarstern towed a camera sled over the floor of Antarctica's southern Weddell Sea and kept finding round fish nests. They covered at least 240 square kilometres: about 60 million nests, most guarded by one adult icefish with more than 1,700 eggs. Weddell seals dive to these depths, perhaps to feed on the largest fish breeding colony ever found.

source.name: EurekAlert (Cell Press): A vast icefish breeding colony discovered in the Antarctic

title: Sponges Feeding on a Vanished World
place: Langseth Ridge seamounts, Central Arctic Ocean
text: In 2016 the icebreaker Polarstern reached seamounts on the Langseth Ridge, near 87°N under year-round sea ice. Cameras revealed the densest Arctic sponge garden yet found, with adults averaging about 300 years old. With almost no food sinking from above, the sponges seem to live partly on a mat of empty tubeworm tubes, leftovers of a seep community that died out thousands of years ago.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Giant sponge grounds of Central Arctic seamounts are associated with extinct seep life

title: A Chance Meeting at Cape Flora
place: Cape Flora, Northbrook Island, Franz Josef Land, Russia
text: In March 1895, Fridtjof Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen left the drifting Fram with dog sledges, aiming for the North Pole. Constantly shifting pack ice forced them back on 9 April at 86°14′N. They wintered in a crude hut on Franz Josef Land, then paddled lashed-together kayaks along the coast. On 17 June 1896, by sheer coincidence, they met British explorer Frederick Jackson at Cape Flora.

source.name: Fram Museum: The First Fram Expedition (1893-1896)

title: Three Flags Dropped on the Pole
place: North Pole, Arctic Ocean
text: On 11 May 1926 the airship Norge, about 106 metres long, lifted off from Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard with Roald Amundsen, Lincoln Ellsworth, pilot Umberto Nobile and his dog Titina aboard. Early next morning it crossed the North Pole, and the crew dropped Norwegian, American and Italian flags onto the ice. After fog coated it in ice, the Norge landed near Teller, Alaska, about 72 hours after leaving.

source.name: Fram Museum: The Norge flight (1926)

title: Stranded Seaplanes Near the Pole
place: Drift ice near 87°43′N, Arctic Ocean
text: In May 1925, Roald Amundsen and five men flew two seaplanes, N24 and N25, north from Svalbard. After eight hours they came down on leads in the drift ice at 87°43′N, and N24 was too damaged to fly again. For about three and a half weeks they lived crammed in N25, clearing runways that the shifting ice kept wrecking. On 15 June, all six squeezed aboard and took off.

source.name: Fram Museum: The N24/N25 flight towards the North Pole (1925)

title: The Islands Norway Never Kept
place: Axel Heiberg Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: From 1898 to 1902, Otto Sverdrup took the Fram into Canada's high Arctic and stayed four winters, the last because Goose Fjord's ice refused to break up. His crew mapped about 200,000 square kilometres of unknown land, including Axel Heiberg Island. Sverdrup claimed it all for Norway's king, but Norway's government never followed up. The islands became Canadian, and in 1930 Canada paid Sverdrup for his maps.

source.name: Fram Museum: The Second Fram Expedition (1898-1902)

title: A Continent Set Aside for Peace
place: Antarctica (treaty signed in Washington, DC, USA)
text: On 1 December 1959, twelve countries whose scientists had worked in Antarctica during the International Geophysical Year signed a treaty in Washington. It declared the continent for peaceful purposes only, guaranteed freedom of scientific research and required results to be shared openly. Rival territorial claims were frozen, with no new ones allowed. The treaty took effect in 1961, and 58 countries are now parties to it.

source.name: Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty: The Antarctic Treaty

title: Three Penguin Eggs in the Dark
place: Cape Crozier, Ross Island, Antarctica
text: On 27 June 1911, in the total darkness of Antarctic winter, Edward Wilson, Birdie Bowers and Apsley Cherry-Garrard set off to collect emperor penguin eggs at Cape Crozier. Temperatures fell as low as minus 68°C. Wilson hoped the embryos would link birds to reptiles. Two of five eggs cracked; three survived, but proved scientifically disappointing. Today they sit in London's Natural History Museum as relics of extraordinary effort.

source.name: The Scientist: Harrowing Egg Hunt, 1911

title: Norse Ivory Hunters in the Far North
place: Pikialasorsuaq (North Water Polynya), between Greenland and Ellesmere Island
text: Medieval Norse Greenlanders shipped walrus ivory to Europe as tusks still fixed to the front of the skull. Ancient DNA from 31 ivory pieces now shows where those walruses lived. After about 1120 CE, close to half came from the North Water, a High Arctic hunting ground some 30 days' sail from Norse farms, where Tuniit and Thule Inuit hunted too, making encounters almost certain.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Greenland Norse walrus exploitation deep into the Arctic

title: Young Nelson Versus the Polar Bear
place: Pack ice north of Spitsbergen, Svalbard, Norway
text: In 1773 the Royal Navy ships Racehorse and Carcass sailed north of Spitsbergen to test whether the open sea itself froze, hoping for a route over the pole to the East Indies. Pack ice drove them back. According to a famous tale, young midshipman Horatio Nelson stalked a polar bear across the ice. His musket misfired, he swung its butt, and a crack in the ice saved him.

source.name: Royal Museums Greenwich: Nelson and the bear

source2.name: Captain Cook Memorial Museum: Northward Ho! A Voyage towards the North Pole

title: Graves of the Scurvy-Struck Whalers
place: Likneset, Smeerenburgfjorden, Svalbard, Norway
text: At Likneset, 'Corpse Point', in northwest Svalbard, 225 graves hold European whalers of the 1600s and 1700s, the largest whaling burial ground on the islands. The 20 skeletons excavated were mostly young men, buried in woollen caps, jackets and knitted stockings. Signs of scurvy appear in 18 of 19 studied, and worn spines show brutal labour. Thawing permafrost and erosion are now destroying the graves.

source.name: PLOS One (PMC): Skeletons in the permafrost, the early modern whaling burial site of Likneset, Svalbard

title: Primate Cousins in the Polar Night
place: Margaret Formation near Bay Fiord, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada
text: About 52 million years ago, Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic held swampy forests like the cypress swamps of the southern United States, home to crocodilians and early tapir relatives. Fossil teeth reveal two new species of Ignacius, small early primate cousins, the northernmost ever found. Larger than their southern kin, with jaws built for hard foods, they endured roughly six months of winter darkness.

source.name: PLOS One (PMC): Basal Primatomorpha colonized Ellesmere Island during the early Eocene climatic optimum

title: An Ancient Polar Bear's Genetic Twist
place: Poolepynten, Prins Karls Forland, Svalbard, Norway
text: A polar bear jawbone from Poolepynten on Svalbard dates to the Eemian warm period, 130,000 to 115,000 years ago. In 2022, scientists published a detailed genome from it and compared it with living polar and brown bears from Alaska, where the species increasingly meet. The surprise: ancient genes flowed mainly from brown bears into polar bears, partly reversing the accepted idea that mixing ran the other way.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Insights into bear evolution from a Pleistocene polar bear genome

title: A Crater Hidden Under Greenland's Ice
place: Hiawatha Glacier, northwest Greenland
text: Beneath Hiawatha Glacier in northwest Greenland lies a buried impact crater about 31 kilometres wide. Some scientists suspected it was young, formed after the ice sheet began. To test this, researchers dated meltwater sand and pebbles of impact-melted rock washed out from under the glacier. Shocked zircon crystals gave an age of about 58 million years, long before Greenland's ice sheet existed.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): A Late Paleocene age for Greenland's Hiawatha impact structure

title: Life in a Lake Under the Ice
place: Subglacial Lake Whillans, Whillans Ice Stream, West Antarctica
text: In January 2013, a US-led team used a filtered, UV-sterilised hot-water drill to bore through about 800 metres of West Antarctic ice into Subglacial Lake Whillans. It was the first time anyone had directly sampled water and mud from an Antarctic subglacial lake. Though the lake was only about 2.2 metres deep, its dark water held around 130,000 microbial cells in every millilitre.

source.name: Frontiers in Microbiology (PMC): Microbial Community Structure of Subglacial Lake Whillans, West Antarctica

title: 'Yowza-Yowza': A Rock From Mars
place: Far Western Icefield, Allan Hills, Antarctica
text: On 27 December 1984, during a snowmobile ride across the Far Western Icefield of the Allan Hills, meteorite hunters picked up a greenish-grey stone. The field notes added: 'Yowza-Yowza'. Weighing 1,931 grams, ALH84001 was later recognised as a rock from Mars, more than 4 billion years old. In 1996, a team led by David McKay argued that tiny features inside it might be traces of ancient life.

source.name: NASA Astromaterials Curation: Martian Meteorite Compendium, ALH84001

title: A Secret Wartime Mission South
place: Port Lockroy, Goudier Island, Antarctic Peninsula, Antarctica
text: In February 1944, in the middle of World War II, Britain's secret Operation Tabarin reached Antarctica. Led by James Marr, its men turned a disused whaling station on Deception Island into a base, then, blocked by pack ice at Hope Bay, built Bransfield House at Port Lockroy instead. At Deception they even put up a 'Port Foster Post Office' sign, claiming the farthest south post office.

source.name: British Antarctic Survey: Operation Tabarin

title: Australia's Oldest Antarctic Station
place: Mawson Station, Horseshoe Harbour, Mac. Robertson Land, Antarctica
text: On 13 February 1954, Phillip Law raised the Australian flag at Horseshoe Harbour in East Antarctica and named a new station after explorer Douglas Mawson. He had chosen the rocky site from aerial photographs. Ten men wintered in cramped quarters that first year. Mawson later gained Antarctica's first aircraft hangar and a cosmic ray observatory carved into bedrock, and it is the oldest station south of the Antarctic Circle.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Mawson station history

title: A Station Swallowed by Ice
place: Wilkes Station, Clark Peninsula, Wilkes Land, Antarctica
text: In January 1957, US Navy crews built Wilkes station in East Antarctica in just 16 days, unloading 11,000 tons of material for the International Geophysical Year. Australia took it over in 1959, allowed to use the stores but not remove anything. Leaking fuel and drifting snow soon made it unsafe, and it closed in 1969. Today it lies frozen in ice, revealed only every four or five years.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Wilkes station history

title: Two Messengers Who Never Arrived
place: Winter quarters near Cape Chelyuskin, Taymyr Peninsula, Russia
text: In 1918 Roald Amundsen's new ship Maud sailed the Northeast Passage, hoping to drift across the Arctic Ocean as Nansen's Fram had. Ice trapped it beyond Cape Chelyuskin for its first winter. In September 1919, Peter Tessem and Paul Knudsen left the ship to carry scientific results home to Norway. Neither was seen alive again; remains found later suggest Tessem froze to death near Dikson.

source.name: Fram Museum: The Maud Expedition (1918-1925)
